stem: What does the Fisher-Neyman factorization theorem say about a statistic $T(X)$?
correct: $T$ is sufficient exactly when $f(x\mid\theta)=g(T(x),\theta)\,h(x)$ for some functions $g$ and $h$ with $h$ free of $\theta$.
The density splits into a $\theta$-part seen only through $T$ and a $\theta$-free remainder.

distractors.text: $T$ is sufficient exactly when the distribution of $T(X)$ is the same for every $\theta$.
distractors.misconception: confuses sufficiency with ancillarity

distractors.text: $T$ is sufficient exactly when it is the unbiased estimator of $\theta$ with smallest variance.
distractors.misconception: confuses sufficiency with UMVU optimality

distractors.text: $T$ is sufficient exactly when the likelihood is maximised at $T(x)$ for every sample.
distractors.misconception: confuses sufficiency with the MLE

distractors.text: $T$ is sufficient exactly when $h(x)$ in the factorization depends on $\theta$ only through $T$.
distractors.misconception: misplaces the parameter: $h$ must not involve $\theta$

distractors.text: $T$ is sufficient only when it has the same dimension as the parameter $\theta$.
distractors.misconception: believes a sufficient statistic must match the parameter dimension

explanation: Factorization gives sufficiency: all dependence on $\theta$ passes through $T$, and $h$ is free of $\theta$. Dimensions need not match, and ancillarity is the opposite property.

stem: Why is $U(0,\theta)$ not an exponential family in $\theta$?
correct: Its support $(0,\theta)$ depends on $\theta$, which a density $h(x)\exp\{\eta(\theta)T(x)-A(\theta)\}$ cannot produce.
The set where the density is positive moves with $\theta$, unlike in the exponential form.

distractors.text: Its density is not differentiable with respect to $\theta$ at the points where it is positive.
distractors.misconception: confuses the family form with smoothness

distractors.text: It has no sufficient statistic smaller than the whole sample, so it cannot have the exponential form.
distractors.misconception: ignores that the sample maximum is sufficient

distractors.text: Its density integrates to a value that depends on $\theta$, so it is not a proper density.
distractors.misconception: forgets the normalising factor $1/\theta$

distractors.text: It has more than one unknown parameter, whereas the exponential form allows only one.
distractors.misconception: miscounts parameters (and $k$-parameter families exist)

distractors.text: Its mean $\theta/2$ is not finite, so the cumulant function does not exist.
distractors.misconception: the mean exists; support is the real issue

explanation: The exponential-family form has the same support for all $\theta$. For $U(0,\theta)$ the sample maximum is sufficient, but the support changes, so it is not in the family.

stem: Let $X_1,\dots,X_n$ be an i.i.d. sample from a full-rank exponential family with natural statistic $T$. What can be said about $\sum_i T(X_i)$?
correct: It is a minimal sufficient statistic for the natural parameter, and it is also complete.
It is sufficient, minimal and complete when the natural parameter space contains an open set.

distractors.text: It is sufficient but can never be minimal, because it uses all observations.
distractors.misconception: believes using all data prevents minimality

distractors.text: It is ancillary, since the density does not change shape across observations.
distractors.misconception: confuses sufficiency with ancillarity

distractors.text: It is unbiased for the natural parameter, which makes it the UMVUE of it.
distractors.misconception: confuses a statistic's role with an unbiased estimator of $\eta$

distractors.text: It is sufficient and minimal, but completeness fails whenever the sample size exceeds the dimension.
distractors.misconception: misstates when completeness holds

distractors.text: It is complete only when the sample is normal; for other exponential families it is not.
distractors.misconception: restricts completeness to the normal family

explanation: For full-rank exponential families $\sum T(X_i)$ is complete and sufficient, hence minimal sufficient. Completeness rests on uniqueness of Laplace transforms and needs an open natural parameter set.

stem: A statistic $S(X)$ is called ancillary for $\theta$. What does this mean?
correct: The distribution of $S(X)$ is exactly the same for every value of $\theta$ in the parameter space.
$S$ has a law free of $\theta$, so alone it carries no information about it.

distractors.text: $S$ is a function of every sufficient statistic, so it is as informative as the whole sample.
distractors.misconception: confuses with being a function of a minimal sufficient statistic

distractors.text: $S$ has expectation zero for every $\theta$, so it is an unbiased estimator of zero.
distractors.misconception: confuses ancillarity with mean zero

distractors.text: $S$ is independent of every other statistic computed from the same sample.
distractors.misconception: overstates; independence needs completeness (Basu)

distractors.text: $S$ carries all the information about $\theta$ available in the sample.
distractors.misconception: reverses the meaning

distractors.text: $S$ is a sufficient statistic whose dimension is smaller than that of the sample.
distractors.misconception: confuses with data reduction by sufficiency

explanation: Ancillary means the law of $S$ does not involve $\theta$. Ancillary statistics need not be independent of a sufficient one unless the sufficient statistic is complete (Basu).

stem: Let $X_1,\dots,X_n$ be i.i.d. $N(\theta,1)$ with $n\ge2$. Which statistic is ancillary for $\theta$?
correct: $X_1-\bar X$, since it has the $N(0,1-1/n)$ law whatever $\theta$ is, and so is ancillary.
The first deviation from the mean, since its law is free of $\theta$ for every $n\ge2$.

distractors.text: The sample mean $\bar X$, since its variance $1/n$ does not depend on $\theta$.
distractors.misconception: only the variance is free of $\theta$; the law of $\bar X$ is not

distractors.text: The sum of squares $\sum_i X_i^2$, because it is a symmetric function of the sample.
distractors.misconception: symmetry does not remove dependence on $\theta$

distractors.text: The sample maximum $\max_i X_i$, because the order of the data is irrelevant.
distractors.misconception: its law shifts with $\theta$

distractors.text: The statistic $\bar X+X_1-\bar X$, because the two pieces are independent.
distractors.misconception: the sum is $X_1$, which depends on $\theta$

distractors.text: The sample mean $\bar X$, because it is sufficient and so cannot depend on $\theta$.
distractors.misconception: confuses sufficiency with ancillarity

explanation: Subtracting the mean removes the location: $X_1-\bar X$ depends only on the $N(0,1)$ errors. By Basu it is independent of the complete sufficient $\bar X$.

stem: What does it mean for a statistic $T$ to be complete?
correct: If $E_\theta g(T)=0$ for every $\theta$, then $g(T)=0$ with probability one under every $\theta$.
No nonzero function of $T$ is an unbiased estimator of zero.

distractors.text: If $E_\theta g(T)=0$ for some single $\theta$, then $g(T)=0$ almost surely.
distractors.misconception: drops the requirement of holding for all $\theta$

distractors.text: $T$ is a function of every other sufficient statistic, so no data reduction is possible.
distractors.misconception: confuses completeness with minimal sufficiency

distractors.text: $T$ has the same distribution for all $\theta$, so $E_\theta g(T)$ is constant.
distractors.misconception: confuses completeness with ancillarity

distractors.text: $T$ is an unbiased estimator of $\theta$ with the smallest possible variance.
distractors.misconception: confuses completeness with UMVU

distractors.text: Every unbiased estimator of $\theta$ that depends on $T$ has the same variance.
distractors.misconception: misreads uniqueness of unbiased functions as equal variance

explanation: Completeness says the only unbiased estimator of zero based on $T$ is zero. It gives uniqueness of unbiased estimators that are functions of $T$.

stem: Let $T$ be complete and sufficient and let $h(T)$ be unbiased for $g(\theta)$. What does the Lehmann-Scheffe theorem conclude?
correct: $h(T)$ is the unique UMVUE of $g(\theta)$, having the smallest variance among all unbiased estimators.
No unbiased estimator of $g(\theta)$ has smaller variance than $h(T)$ at any $\theta$.

distractors.text: $h(T)$ has the smallest mean squared error among all estimators, including biased ones.
distractors.misconception: extends optimality beyond unbiased estimators

distractors.text: $h(T)$ has minimum variance only among those unbiased estimators that are functions of $T$.
distractors.misconception: misses that Rao-Blackwell extends it to all unbiased estimators

distractors.text: $h(T)$ attains the Cramer-Rao lower bound for every $\theta$ and every sample size.
distractors.misconception: assumes the bound is always attained

distractors.text: $h(T)$ is a UMVUE, but other UMVUEs of $g(\theta)$ exist that differ with positive probability.
distractors.misconception: ignores uniqueness

distractors.text: $h(T)$ is the maximum likelihood estimator of $g(\theta)$.
distractors.misconception: confuses the UMVUE with the MLE

explanation: With completeness, Rao-Blackwell improves any unbiased estimator to a function of $T$, and completeness makes that function unique. So $h(T)$ is the best unbiased estimator.

stem: Which statement about Rao-Blackwellization is correct? Here $\delta(X)$ is unbiased for $g(\theta)$ and $T$ is sufficient.
correct: $E[\delta\mid T]$ is unbiased and has variance no larger than that of $\delta$.
Conditioning an unbiased estimator on $T$ never raises its variance.

distractors.text: $E[\delta(X)\mid T]$ always has strictly smaller variance than $\delta(X)$.
distractors.misconception: ignores the equality case when $\delta$ is already a function of $T$

distractors.text: $E[\delta(X)\mid T]$ reduces the variance but introduces bias that vanishes as $n$ grows.
distractors.misconception: believes conditioning induces bias

distractors.text: The result needs $T$ to be complete, otherwise $E[\delta(X)\mid T]$ may depend on $\theta$.
distractors.misconception: confuses sufficiency with completeness

distractors.text: The result holds for any statistic $T$, because conditioning always reduces variance.
distractors.misconception: forgets that sufficiency makes the conditional expectation computable without $\theta$

distractors.text: $E[\delta(X)\mid T]$ is the maximum likelihood estimator of $g(\theta)$.
distractors.misconception: confuses Rao-Blackwellization with maximum likelihood

explanation: Sufficiency makes $E[\delta\mid T]$ free of $\theta$, hence an estimator. Unbiasedness follows from the tower rule and variance does not increase by the law of total variance.

stem: Basu's theorem concerns a complete sufficient statistic $T$ and an ancillary statistic $S$. What does it assert?
correct: $T$ and $S$ are independent under every value of $\theta$.
Complete sufficient and ancillary statistics are independent.

distractors.text: Any sufficient statistic is independent of any ancillary statistic.
distractors.misconception: drops the completeness requirement

distractors.text: $S$ is a function of $T$, so the two are perfectly dependent.
distractors.misconception: reverses the conclusion

distractors.text: $T$ and $S$ are independent only at the value $\theta$ where $S$ has mean zero.
distractors.misconception: restricts independence to one $\theta$

distractors.text: $T$ and $S$ are uncorrelated but may still be dependent.
distractors.misconception: weakens independence to zero correlation

distractors.text: $T$ is independent of all unbiased estimators of $\theta$.
distractors.misconception: confuses ancillary statistics with unbiased estimators

explanation: Basu gives full independence. A standard use: for normal samples with known variance, $\bar X$ is complete sufficient and $S^2$ is ancillary, so $\bar X$ and $S^2$ are independent.

stem: For $X_1,\dots,X_n$ i.i.d. Poisson($\lambda$), why does $\mathbf 1\{X_1=0\}$ help in finding the UMVUE of $e^{-\lambda}$?
correct: It is unbiased for $e^{-\lambda}$, so conditioning it on the complete sufficient statistic $\sum_iX_i$ gives the UMVUE.
Rao-Blackwellizing it by the sum $\sum_iX_i$ gives the UMVUE, a function of that sum.

distractors.text: It is itself a function of the complete sufficient statistic, so it is already the UMVUE.
distractors.misconception: misses that the indicator depends on $X_1$ alone

distractors.text: Its conditional expectation given $\sum_i X_i$ equals $e^{-\bar X}$, which is therefore the UMVUE.
distractors.misconception: confuses plug-in with the conditional expectation, which is biased

distractors.text: It is ancillary for $\lambda$, so by Basu's theorem it is independent of the sample mean.
distractors.misconception: misidentifies it as ancillary; its mean depends on $\lambda$

distractors.text: It is consistent for $e^{-\lambda}$, and consistency suffices for being the UMVUE.
distractors.misconception: confuses consistency with optimality

distractors.text: It is the maximum likelihood estimator of $e^{-\lambda}$ based on the first observation.
distractors.misconception: confuses unbiased indicator with an MLE

explanation: The indicator is unbiased; $E[\mathbf 1\{X_1=0\}\mid\sum X_i=s]=(1-1/n)^s$, a function of the complete sufficient statistic, hence the UMVUE. The plug-in $e^{-\bar X}$ is biased.

stem: Under regularity conditions, which expression gives the Fisher information $I(\theta)$ of one observation?
correct: $I(\theta)=\operatorname{Var}_\theta\{\partial_\theta\log f(X\mid\theta)\}=-E_\theta[\partial^2_\theta\log f(X\mid\theta)]$.
The score variance, i.e. minus the expected Hessian of $\log f$.

distractors.text: $I(\theta)=E_\theta\!\left[\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\log f(X\mid\theta)\right]$, the expected score.
distractors.misconception: the expected score is zero, not the information

distractors.text: $I(\theta)=E_\theta\!\left[\frac{\partial^2}{\partial\theta^2}\log f(X\mid\theta)\right]$, without the minus sign.
distractors.misconception: sign error: this expectation is non-positive

distractors.text: $I(\theta)=1/\operatorname{Var}_\theta(X)$ for every regular model.
distractors.misconception: true only in special models such as the normal mean

distractors.text: $I(\theta)=\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\log f(x\mid\theta)$ evaluated at the observed value $x$.
distractors.misconception: confuses the observed score with its variance

distractors.text: $I(\theta)=E_\theta\{(X-\theta)^2\}$, the mean squared deviation of the observation from the parameter.
distractors.misconception: confuses information with the variance of the data

explanation: Information is the variance of the score, which has mean zero, and equals the negative expected Hessian. The identity needs differentiation under the integral sign.

stem: For $n$ i.i.d. observations with one-observation information $I_1(\theta)$, what is the information $I_n(\theta)$ in the whole sample?
correct: $I_n(\theta)=n\,I_1(\theta)$, since the scores of independent observations add and so do their variances.
It grows linearly with the sample size, as $n$ times $I_1$.

distractors.text: $I_n(\theta)=\sqrt n\,I_1(\theta)$, because standard errors scale like $\sqrt n$.
distractors.misconception: confuses scaling of information with that of standard error

distractors.text: $I_n(\theta)=I_1(\theta)/n$, because averaging reduces the information per observation.
distractors.misconception: confuses information with the variance of the mean

distractors.text: $I_n(\theta)=I_1(\theta)$, because all observations concern the same parameter.
distractors.misconception: ignores that independent observations add information

distractors.text: $I_n(\theta)=n^2I_1(\theta)$, because the log-likelihood is a sum of $n$ terms.
distractors.misconception: squares the sample size instead of summing variances

distractors.text: $I_n(\theta)=I_1(\theta)^n$, because the joint density is a product of $n$ densities.
distractors.misconception: turns the sum of log-likelihood terms into a power

explanation: The log-likelihood is a sum, so the score is a sum of independent terms with variance $nI_1(\theta)$. The estimator's variance bound therefore shrinks like $1/n$.

stem: Which statement of the Cramer-Rao inequality is correct under regularity conditions?
correct: Any unbiased estimator $T$ of $g(\theta)$ satisfies $\operatorname{Var}_\theta(T)\ge g'(\theta)^2/I_n(\theta)$.
Unbiasedness forces the variance to be at least $g'(\theta)^2/I_n(\theta)$.

distractors.text: Any estimator of $\theta$, biased or not, satisfies $\operatorname{Var}_\theta(T)\ge1/I_n(\theta)$.
distractors.misconception: applies the unbiased bound to biased estimators

distractors.text: Any unbiased estimator of $g(\theta)$ satisfies $\operatorname{Var}_\theta(T)\le g'(\theta)^2/I_n(\theta)$.
distractors.misconception: reverses the inequality

distractors.text: Any unbiased estimator of $g(\theta)$ satisfies $\operatorname{Var}_\theta(T)\ge g(\theta)^2/I_n(\theta)$.
distractors.misconception: replaces the derivative $g'$ by $g$

distractors.text: The bound holds for every statistical model, including those whose support depends on $\theta$.
distractors.misconception: ignores the regularity conditions

distractors.text: Any unbiased estimator of $g(\theta)$ satisfies $\operatorname{Var}_\theta(T)\ge g'(\theta)/I_n(\theta)$, with the derivative unsquared.
distractors.misconception: forgets to square the derivative

explanation: Cauchy-Schwarz applied to $\operatorname{Cov}(T,\text{score})=g'(\theta)$ gives the bound. Regularity requires a $\theta$-free support so that integration and differentiation can be exchanged.

stem: When does an unbiased estimator $T$ of $g(\theta)$ attain the Cramer-Rao bound at every $\theta$?
correct: Exactly when the score equals $a(\theta)\{T-g(\theta)\}$ for some function $a(\theta)$, i.e. equality in Cauchy-Schwarz.
When the score is linear in $T$, with $\theta$-only coefficients.

distractors.text: Whenever $T$ is a sufficient statistic for $\theta$.
distractors.misconception: sufficiency does not imply equality in the bound

distractors.text: Whenever $T$ is the UMVUE of $g(\theta)$, since the UMVUE has smallest variance.
distractors.misconception: the UMVUE can have variance above the bound

distractors.text: Whenever $T$ is the maximum likelihood estimator, at every sample size.
distractors.misconception: the MLE attains the bound only asymptotically, if at all

distractors.text: Only when $T$ is a biased estimator, which has smaller variance than any unbiased one.
distractors.misconception: confuses the bound for unbiased estimators with a bias-variance trade-off

distractors.text: Exactly when $T$ is a complete statistic, since completeness forces the smallest possible variance.
distractors.misconception: confuses completeness with equality in Cauchy-Schwarz

explanation: Equality holds iff the score is proportional to $T-g(\theta)$. This forces an exponential family in which $T$ estimates the mean of the natural statistic.

stem: For a normal sample with unknown mean and variance, $S^2$ is the UMVUE of $\sigma^2$. How does its variance compare with the Cramer-Rao bound for $\sigma^2$?
correct: Its variance $2\sigma^4/(n-1)$ is strictly above the bound $2\sigma^4/n$, so a UMVUE need not attain the bound.
It is the best unbiased estimator, yet the bound is not attained at any finite $n$.

distractors.text: It attains the bound exactly for every $n$, since $S^2$ is a function of a complete sufficient statistic.
distractors.misconception: assumes UMVUE implies equality in the bound

distractors.text: It cannot be the UMVUE, since an estimator that misses the bound cannot be optimal.
distractors.misconception: believes the bound must be reached by the best estimator

distractors.text: The bound does not exist, because the mean is unknown and so the information is undefined.
distractors.misconception: ignores that the information matrix is diagonal here

distractors.text: It is the maximum likelihood estimator $\hat\sigma^2$, which is the one that attains the bound.
distractors.misconception: confuses $S^2$ with the biased MLE

distractors.text: It attains the bound at each $n$, because the sample mean attains the bound for estimating $\mu$.
distractors.misconception: transfers attainment from the mean to the variance

explanation: Var$(S^2)=2\sigma^4/(n-1)$ while the bound is $2\sigma^4/n$. Attainment needs the score to be linear in the estimator, which fails when the mean is unknown; $S^2$ is still UMVUE by Lehmann-Scheffe.

stem: Under regularity conditions, what is the asymptotic distribution of the MLE $\hat\theta_n$ from $n$ i.i.d. observations at the true value $\theta_0$?
correct: $\sqrt n(\hat\theta_n-\theta_0)$ converges in distribution to $N\!\left(0,\,1/I_1(\theta_0)\right)$.
The MLE is approximately normal, centred at $\theta_0$ with variance $1/\{nI_1(\theta_0)\}$.

distractors.text: $\sqrt n(\hat\theta_n-\theta_0)$ converges in distribution to $N\!\left(0,\,I_1(\theta_0)\right)$.
distractors.misconception: inverts the information

distractors.text: $\hat\theta_n-\theta_0$ converges in distribution to $N\!\left(0,\,1/I_1(\theta_0)\right)$ without any scaling.
distractors.misconception: forgets the $\sqrt n$ scaling, which would make it degenerate

distractors.text: $\sqrt n(\hat\theta_n-\theta_0)$ converges to a chi-square limit with one degree of freedom.
distractors.misconception: confuses the MLE limit with that of the LRT statistic

distractors.text: The limit holds only if $\hat\theta_n$ is an unbiased estimator of $\theta_0$ for every $n$.
distractors.misconception: requires finite-sample unbiasedness unnecessarily

distractors.text: $\sqrt n(\hat\theta_n-\theta_0)$ converges to $N\!\left(0,\,1/I_1(\theta_0)\right)$ only when the model is a normal location family.
distractors.misconception: restricts a general theorem to the normal case

explanation: The MLE is consistent, asymptotically normal and asymptotically efficient, attaining the Cramer-Rao variance $1/\{nI_1(\theta_0)\}$ in the limit. No finite-sample unbiasedness is needed.

stem: Which of the Wald, score and likelihood ratio statistics for $H_0:\theta=\theta_0$ can be computed using only the fit under the null?
correct: The score statistic $U(\theta_0)^2/I_n(\theta_0)$, which needs only the score and information under the null.
The score statistic, which is evaluated at the null value alone.

distractors.text: The Wald statistic, because it only compares the MLE with $\theta_0$.
distractors.misconception: overlooks that the Wald statistic needs the unrestricted MLE

distractors.text: The likelihood ratio statistic, since it is a function of the null likelihood alone.
distractors.misconception: overlooks the maximised likelihood in the numerator

distractors.text: All three, since they are asymptotically equivalent under the null.
distractors.misconception: asymptotic equivalence does not mean identical inputs

distractors.text: None of them, since every large-sample test needs the maximum likelihood estimator.
distractors.misconception: does not know the score test

distractors.text: The Wald statistic with the information evaluated at $\theta_0$, because that avoids fitting the alternative.
distractors.misconception: the Wald statistic still uses the unrestricted MLE in its numerator

explanation: Wald uses $(\hat\theta-\theta_0)^2I_n(\hat\theta)$, the LRT uses the maximised likelihood, but the score test uses $U(\theta_0)$ and $I_n(\theta_0)$ only. All have a $\chi^2_1$ limit under $H_0$.

stem: Neyman and Scott: $X_{i1},X_{i2}$ are independent $N(\mu_i,\sigma^2)$ for $i=1,\dots,n$. The MLE of $\sigma^2$ converges to $\sigma^2/2$. What does this show?
correct: Consistency of the MLE can fail when the nuisance parameters grow with $n$.
Growing nuisance parameters can destroy consistency.

distractors.text: The MLE of a variance is always inconsistent for normal data.
distractors.misconception: overgeneralises; the MLE is consistent with fixed $\mu$

distractors.text: The bias of the MLE disappears as $n$ grows, so it is consistent after all.
distractors.misconception: the bias does not vanish here

distractors.text: The likelihood is unbounded, so no maximum exists.
distractors.misconception: the likelihood has a maximum, but at the wrong value

distractors.text: The pairs are dependent, so the factorization of the likelihood is invalid.
distractors.misconception: the pairs are independent

distractors.text: Maximum likelihood is inconsistent in every model that has more than one unknown parameter.
distractors.misconception: overgeneralises from a failure with growing dimension

explanation: Each $\mu_i$ is estimated from only two observations, so the within-pair residual variance is underestimated by a factor 2 regardless of $n$. The fixed-dimension assumption fails.

stem: Let $g$ be differentiable with $g'(\theta_0)\neq0$ and let $\hat\theta_n$ be the MLE. What is the asymptotic distribution of $g(\hat\theta_n)$?
correct: Approximately $N\!\left(g(\theta_0),\ g'(\theta_0)^2/\{nI_1(\theta_0)\}\right)$, and $g(\hat\theta_n)$ is the MLE of $g(\theta)$.
By invariance and the delta method, variance $g'(\theta_0)^2/\{nI_1(\theta_0)\}$.

distractors.text: Approximately $N\!\left(g(\theta_0),\ g'(\theta_0)/\{nI_1(\theta_0)\}\right)$, with the derivative unsquared.
distractors.misconception: forgets to square the derivative in the delta method

distractors.text: Approximately $N\!\left(g(\theta_0),\ 1/\{nI_1(g(\theta_0))\}\right)$, using the same information function.
distractors.misconception: ignores the change of parameter in the information

distractors.text: Not normal in general, since a nonlinear map destroys normality.
distractors.misconception: ignores the delta method

distractors.text: Normal, but $g(\hat\theta_n)$ is the MLE of $g(\theta)$ only when $g$ is linear.
distractors.misconception: ignores invariance of the MLE

distractors.text: It is approximately normal with variance $g'(\theta_0)^2\,nI_1(\theta_0)$, since information multiplies the variance.
distractors.misconception: multiplies by the information instead of dividing

explanation: The delta method multiplies the variance by $g'(\theta_0)^2$, and the MLE is invariant under reparametrization. Hence $g(\hat\theta_n)$ is asymptotically efficient for $g(\theta)$.

stem: For a Wald interval for $\theta$, which choice of standard error is justified by the large-sample theory of the MLE?
correct: Either observed information $-\ell''(\hat\theta)$ or expected $nI_1(\hat\theta)$, both evaluated at the MLE.
Either the observed or the expected information, evaluated at the MLE.

distractors.text: $1/\sqrt{nI_1(\theta_0)}$ with the true value, which is the only valid choice.
distractors.misconception: believes plug-in of the MLE is invalid

distractors.text: $1/\{nI_1(\hat\theta)\}$ without the square root, because information is a variance.
distractors.misconception: confuses the information with its square root in the standard error

distractors.text: Only the expected information, because the observed information is random.
distractors.misconception: ignores that the observed information is consistent for it

distractors.text: The sample standard deviation of the data divided by $\sqrt n$, in every model.
distractors.misconception: applies the normal-mean formula to all models

distractors.text: The reciprocal of the maximised log-likelihood $\ell(\hat\theta)$, since a larger likelihood means a smaller error.
distractors.misconception: confuses the height of the likelihood with its curvature

explanation: Both $-\ell''(\hat\theta)/n$ and $I_1(\hat\theta)$ converge to $I_1(\theta_0)$, so replacing the unknown information by either at the MLE preserves the normal limit by Slutsky.

stem: What is the risk function $R(\theta,\delta)$ of a decision rule $\delta$ with loss $L$?
correct: $E_\theta\{L(\theta,\delta(X))\}$, the expected loss over repeated samples at a fixed $\theta$.
The average loss of the rule over the sampling distribution.

distractors.text: $R(\theta,\delta)=L(\theta,\delta(x))$ evaluated at the single observed sample $x$.
distractors.misconception: confuses loss with risk

distractors.text: $R(\theta,\delta)=\int R(\theta,\delta)\,\pi(\theta)\,d\theta$, the average over a prior.
distractors.misconception: confuses risk with Bayes risk

distractors.text: $R(\theta,\delta)=\operatorname{Var}_\theta(\delta(X))$, the sampling variance of the rule.
distractors.misconception: equates risk with variance, ignoring bias

distractors.text: $R(\theta,\delta)=E\{L(\theta,\delta(X))\mid X=x\}$, the expected loss given the data.
distractors.misconception: confuses frequentist risk with posterior expected loss

distractors.text: $R(\theta,\delta)=\sup_x L(\theta,\delta(x))$, the largest loss over all possible samples.
distractors.misconception: confuses risk with the worst-case loss

explanation: Risk averages the loss over the sampling distribution of $X$, with $\theta$ held fixed. A rule is judged by the whole function $\theta\mapsto R(\theta,\delta)$.

stem: Under squared error loss, how does the risk of an estimator $\delta$ of $\theta$ decompose?
correct: Risk equals the variance of the estimator plus the square of its bias.
The risk is the variance plus the bias squared, for every estimator.

distractors.text: $R(\theta,\delta)=\operatorname{Var}_\theta(\delta)+\operatorname{bias}_\theta(\delta)$, with the bias unsquared.
distractors.misconception: forgets to square the bias

distractors.text: $R(\theta,\delta)=\operatorname{Var}_\theta(\delta)-\{\operatorname{bias}_\theta(\delta)\}^2$, so bias can reduce the risk.
distractors.misconception: sign error

distractors.text: $R(\theta,\delta)=\operatorname{Var}_\theta(\delta)$, because the loss is centred at the true value.
distractors.misconception: ignores the bias term

distractors.text: $R(\theta,\delta)=\{\operatorname{bias}_\theta(\delta)\}^2$ for unbiased and biased estimators alike.
distractors.misconception: drops the variance

distractors.text: The identity $R(\theta,\delta)=\operatorname{Var}_\theta(\delta)+\{\operatorname{bias}_\theta(\delta)\}^2$ holds only for normal data.
distractors.misconception: believes the decomposition needs normality

explanation: $E(\delta-\theta)^2=\operatorname{Var}(\delta)+(E\delta-\theta)^2$. A small bias can be worthwhile if it reduces the variance more, so unbiased rules are not always best.

stem: When is a decision rule $\delta$ inadmissible?
correct: Another rule has no larger risk anywhere and smaller risk somewhere.
It is dominated: some other rule is never worse and sometimes better.

distractors.text: Exactly when some rule $\delta'$ has $R(\theta,\delta')<R(\theta,\delta)$ at every single $\theta$.
distractors.misconception: demands strict improvement everywhere

distractors.text: Some rule $\delta'$ has smaller risk at the true value of $\theta$ for the data observed.
distractors.misconception: compares at one unknown $\theta$ only

distractors.text: The maximum risk of $\delta$ over $\theta$ exceeds that of another rule $\delta'$.
distractors.misconception: confuses inadmissible with not minimax

distractors.text: The rule $\delta$ is biased, so an unbiased rule must dominate it.
distractors.misconception: confuses bias with inadmissibility

distractors.text: Some rule $\delta'$ has smaller risk than $\delta$ when averaged over a given prior $\pi$.
distractors.misconception: confuses admissibility with a Bayes risk comparison

explanation: Admissibility is about domination across all $\theta$. A rule beaten at some $\theta$ and beating the other at another $\theta$ is not dominated. Large maximum risk does not imply inadmissibility.

stem: Under squared error loss, with a model whose distributions are mutually absolutely continuous, is the constant estimator $\delta(X)\equiv c$ admissible for $\theta$?
correct: Yes: its risk is zero at $\theta=c$, so any rival with no larger risk there must equal $c$.
Zero risk at $\theta=c$ leaves no room for a dominating rule.

distractors.text: No, because it ignores the data and so is dominated by the sample mean.
distractors.misconception: the sample mean has positive risk at $\theta=c$

distractors.text: No, because it is biased for every $\theta\neq c$ and bias implies inadmissibility.
distractors.misconception: confuses bias with inadmissibility

distractors.text: Yes, but only when $c=0$, which is the sole value with zero risk.
distractors.misconception: every value $c$ gives zero risk at $\theta=c$

distractors.text: No, because its maximum risk over $\theta$ is infinite, hence it is not minimax.
distractors.misconception: confuses maximum risk with admissibility

distractors.text: No, because shrinking $c$ towards the sample mean gives an estimator with smaller risk.
distractors.misconception: the shrunk estimator has positive risk at $\theta=c$

explanation: Admissibility is a weak property, satisfied by silly rules. A dominating rule would need zero risk at $\theta=c$, and so would equal $c$ a.s. under $P_c$ and hence under all $P_\theta$.

stem: Under which condition can randomised rules be dispensed with, in the sense that some non-randomised rule has risk no larger?
correct: When the loss $L(\theta,a)$ is convex in the action $a$, by Jensen's inequality.
Convex loss lets the mean action replace the random one.

distractors.text: When the loss is the 0-1 loss, as in hypothesis testing.
distractors.misconception: randomised tests are needed for exact size with 0-1 loss

distractors.text: When the parameter space is finite.
distractors.misconception: finiteness of $\Theta$ does not remove the benefit of randomising

distractors.text: When the rule is admissible, because admissible rules are non-randomised.
distractors.misconception: admissible rules can be randomised

distractors.text: Never, because randomisation always strictly lowers the risk.
distractors.misconception: over-states the benefit of randomisation

distractors.text: When the sample space is discrete, since only then can the randomisation be absorbed.
distractors.misconception: invents a condition on the sample space

explanation: For convex loss, replacing a random action by its mean does not increase expected loss (Jensen). With 0-1 loss the action set is not convex, which is why randomised tests are needed.

stem: Under absolute error loss $|\theta-a|$, what is the Bayes estimator?
correct: The posterior median of $\theta$ given the data.
The value splitting the posterior distribution into two halves of mass $1/2$.

distractors.text: The posterior mean of $\theta$ given the data.
distractors.misconception: this is the Bayes rule for squared error loss

distractors.text: The posterior mode of $\theta$ given the data.
distractors.misconception: this arises as a limit of 0-1 loss

distractors.text: The median of the prior distribution of $\theta$.
distractors.misconception: ignores the data

distractors.text: The maximum likelihood estimate, which is also the posterior median in every model.
distractors.misconception: confuses the MLE with a posterior summary

distractors.text: The midpoint of the posterior 2.5% and 97.5% quantiles.
distractors.misconception: confuses the centre of an interval with a Bayes estimator

explanation: Squared error gives the posterior mean, absolute error the posterior median and 0-1 loss the posterior mode. They coincide only for symmetric unimodal posteriors.

stem: How is a Bayes rule with respect to a prior $\pi$ characterised?
correct: It minimises the posterior expected loss at each observed $x$.
It minimises the prior-averaged risk, found pointwise in $x$.

distractors.text: It minimises the maximum over $\theta$ of the risk function.
distractors.misconception: confuses a Bayes rule with a minimax rule

distractors.text: It minimises the risk $R(\theta,\delta)$ at every $\theta$ simultaneously.
distractors.misconception: no rule is uniformly best in general

distractors.text: It minimises the prior expected loss before any data are observed.
distractors.misconception: ignores conditioning on the data

distractors.text: It is unbiased for $\theta$ under the prior and has the smallest variance.
distractors.misconception: confuses Bayes rules with UMVU estimators

distractors.text: It always has risk $R(\theta,\delta)$ that is constant in $\theta$.
distractors.misconception: confuses a Bayes rule with an equaliser rule

explanation: Bayes risk equals the expected posterior expected loss, so minimising the posterior expected loss pointwise in $x$ minimises it. Maximum risk is the minimax criterion instead.

stem: What does it mean for a decision rule $\delta^*$ to be minimax?
correct: It minimises the worst-case risk, that is the supremum over $\theta$ of $R(\theta,\delta)$ among all rules.
Its worst-case risk is the smallest among all rules.

distractors.text: It minimises the Bayes risk $\int R(\theta,\delta)\pi(\theta)d\theta$ under a chosen prior $\pi$.
distractors.misconception: confuses minimax with Bayes

distractors.text: It has the smallest risk at the true value of $\theta$ for the data observed.
distractors.misconception: compares at one unknown $\theta$ only

distractors.text: It has the smallest variance among all unbiased estimators of $\theta$.
distractors.misconception: confuses minimax with UMVU

distractors.text: Its risk equals zero at some value of $\theta$ in the parameter space.
distractors.misconception: confuses minimaxity with zero risk at a point

distractors.text: Its risk is constant in $\theta$ and equal to its Bayes risk under a fixed prior.
distractors.misconception: confuses minimaxity with having constant risk

explanation: Minimax guards against the worst case and is pessimistic. It can differ from the Bayes rule for any natural prior, and it need not be unique.

stem: A Bayes rule $\delta_\pi$ has risk $R(\theta,\delta_\pi)\le r_\pi$ for all $\theta$, where $r_\pi$ is its Bayes risk. What follows?
correct: $\delta_\pi$ is minimax and $\pi$ is a least favourable prior.
A constant-risk Bayes rule is minimax.

distractors.text: $\delta_\pi$ is minimax only if $\pi$ is the uniform prior.
distractors.misconception: minimaxity holds for any such $\pi$

distractors.text: $\delta_\pi$ is minimax but $\pi$ is not least favourable.
distractors.misconception: the bound makes $\pi$ least favourable

distractors.text: Every minimax rule must then have constant risk.
distractors.misconception: reverses the implication; minimax rules need not have constant risk

distractors.text: $\delta_\pi$ is unbiased because its risk does not vary with $\theta$.
distractors.misconception: confuses constant risk with unbiasedness

distractors.text: $\delta_\pi$ is the unique Bayes rule for every other prior as well.
distractors.misconception: confuses a Bayes rule for one prior with one for all priors

explanation: For any rule $\delta$, $\sup_\theta R(\theta,\delta)\ge\int R\,d\pi\ge r_\pi\ge\sup_\theta R(\theta,\delta_\pi)$. Hence $\delta_\pi$ is minimax and $\pi$ least favourable. The converse need not hold.

stem: Which statement about Bayes rules, admissibility and minimaxity is correct?
correct: A unique Bayes rule for a proper prior is admissible.
Uniqueness of the Bayes rule for a proper prior rules out domination.

distractors.text: Every minimax rule is admissible.
distractors.misconception: minimax rules can be dominated

distractors.text: Every Bayes rule for an improper prior is admissible.
distractors.misconception: improper priors may give inadmissible rules

distractors.text: Every admissible rule is a Bayes rule for some proper prior.
distractors.misconception: admissible rules can be limits of Bayes rules

distractors.text: A Bayes rule is minimax for every prior with full support.
distractors.misconception: only particular least favourable priors give minimax rules

distractors.text: A Bayes rule is admissible only if its Bayes risk is exactly zero.
distractors.misconception: invents a condition

explanation: A dominating rule would have Bayes risk no larger, contradicting uniqueness. The converse fails: admissible rules may be only limits of Bayes rules (for example $\bar X$ for a normal mean).

stem: What is a conjugate prior for a given likelihood?
correct: A prior family such that the posterior also belongs to the same family for every sample.
Updating a member of the family returns a member of that family.

distractors.text: A prior that has no influence on the posterior whatever the data.
distractors.misconception: confuses conjugacy with noninformativeness

distractors.text: A prior whose mean equals the maximum likelihood estimate of the data.
distractors.misconception: confuses with empirical Bayes

distractors.text: A prior that is flat over the whole parameter space.
distractors.misconception: confuses conjugacy with uniform priors

distractors.text: A prior that makes the posterior mean equal to the prior mean.
distractors.misconception: ignores learning from the data

distractors.text: A prior whose density is bounded, so that the integral in Bayes' theorem converges.
distractors.misconception: confuses conjugacy with properness

explanation: Conjugacy is a convenience: for example Beta priors with binomial data give Beta posteriors. It is about closure under updating, not about neutrality of the prior.

stem: With a $\mathrm{Beta}(\alpha,\beta)$ prior and $k$ successes in $n$ Bernoulli trials, how does the posterior mean relate to the prior mean and the sample proportion?
correct: An average of prior mean and $k/n$, weight $n/(\alpha+\beta+n)$ on data.
The weight on the data tends to 1 as the sample size grows.

distractors.text: It equals $k/n$ for every choice of $\alpha$ and $\beta$.
distractors.misconception: ignores the prior

distractors.text: It is a weighted average whose weight on the prior grows with $n$.
distractors.misconception: reverses the effect of sample size

distractors.text: It lies outside the interval between the prior mean and $k/n$ when $n$ is large.
distractors.misconception: it always lies between them

distractors.text: It equals $(k+\alpha)/n$, since the prior adds only successes.
distractors.misconception: forgets that the denominator grows by $\alpha+\beta$

distractors.text: It is a weighted average of $\alpha/\beta$ and $k/n$ with weight $n/(\alpha+\beta+n)$ on the data.
distractors.misconception: uses the wrong prior mean, which is $\alpha/(\alpha+\beta)$

explanation: The posterior is $\mathrm{Beta}(\alpha+k,\beta+n-k)$ with mean $(\alpha+k)/(\alpha+\beta+n)$, a convex combination of $\alpha/(\alpha+\beta)$ and $k/n$ with data weight $n/(\alpha+\beta+n)$.

stem: How does a 95% credible interval differ from a 95% confidence interval?
correct: Credible is a probability for $\theta$ given the data; confidence is long-run coverage.
Posterior probability for $\theta$ versus long-run coverage of the procedure.

distractors.text: They have the same interpretation, and only the calculation differs.
distractors.misconception: conflates the two interpretations

distractors.text: A confidence interval contains $\theta$ with probability 0.95 given the observed data.
distractors.misconception: misreads confidence as a posterior probability

distractors.text: A credible interval always has exactly 95% frequentist coverage for every $\theta$.
distractors.misconception: credible intervals have no guaranteed coverage

distractors.text: A 95% credible interval is unique for a given posterior.
distractors.misconception: equal-tailed and highest posterior density intervals can differ

distractors.text: Credible intervals can be used only for large samples, whereas confidence intervals have no such limit.
distractors.misconception: credible intervals are exact in any sample size

explanation: The credible interval treats $\theta$ as random given the data; the confidence interval treats the data as random for fixed $\theta$. Credible intervals need not have exact frequentist coverage.

stem: What does the Bernstein-von Mises theorem say about the posterior in regular models with a prior positive near the true value?
correct: The posterior is about $N(\hat\theta,1/\{nI_1(\hat\theta)\})$ for large $n$.
Credible intervals and Wald intervals agree asymptotically.

distractors.text: The posterior converges to the prior as $n$ grows.
distractors.misconception: reverses the direction: data dominate the prior

distractors.text: The result holds even when the prior gives zero mass to the true parameter.
distractors.misconception: a prior with zero mass near $\theta_0$ cannot be overcome

distractors.text: The posterior variance stays of order one however large $n$ is.
distractors.misconception: the posterior concentrates at rate $1/\sqrt n$

distractors.text: The result holds only for normal likelihoods.
distractors.misconception: it holds for regular models generally

distractors.text: The posterior mean stays a fixed distance from the MLE, set by the prior, however large $n$ is.
distractors.misconception: the prior's influence vanishes

explanation: Under regularity, the posterior is asymptotically normal around the MLE with variance $1/(nI)$. Prior influence vanishes, so credible intervals have asymptotically correct frequentist coverage.

stem: For $X_i\sim N(\theta,\sigma^2)$ with known $\sigma^2$ and the improper flat prior $\pi(\theta)\propto1$, what is the posterior?
correct: A proper normal posterior with mean $\bar x$ and variance $\sigma^2/n$, for every $n$.
The z interval is then the 95% credible interval.

distractors.text: An improper distribution, since the prior is improper.
distractors.misconception: improper priors may still give proper posteriors

distractors.text: $N(0,\sigma^2)$, because the flat prior pulls the posterior mean towards zero.
distractors.misconception: a flat prior does not shrink

distractors.text: $N(\bar x,\sigma^2)$, with the variance not reduced by the sample size.
distractors.misconception: forgets that the data's precision adds up

distractors.text: $N(\bar x,\sigma^2/n)$ only when $n$ is large.
distractors.misconception: the result is exact for every $n$

distractors.text: No usable posterior exists, because Bayes' theorem requires the prior to be a proper density.
distractors.misconception: Bayes' theorem can still be applied formally

explanation: The likelihood is proportional to a normal density in $\theta$, which integrates to a finite value, so the posterior is proper. Improper priors can give improper posteriors in other models.

stem: What does the Neyman-Pearson lemma say for testing a simple $H_0:f_0$ against a simple $H_1:f_1$ at level $\alpha$?
correct: Reject for large $f_1/f_0$, with $k$ set so that the size is $\alpha$ (randomising on ties).
A large likelihood ratio $f_1/f_0$ rejects, at size $\alpha$.

distractors.text: The test rejecting when $f_0(x)/f_1(x)>k$ is most powerful.
distractors.misconception: inverts the likelihood ratio

distractors.text: The most powerful test rejects when $|x|$ is large, in every model.
distractors.misconception: ignores the model

distractors.text: The most powerful test minimises the size subject to a fixed power.
distractors.misconception: reverses the roles of size and power

distractors.text: The lemma applies only when both hypotheses are composite.
distractors.misconception: it concerns simple hypotheses

distractors.text: The critical value $k$ is chosen so that the power, not the size, equals $1-\alpha$.
distractors.misconception: the size constraint fixes $k$

explanation: Reject for large $f_1/f_0$; $k$ is chosen so the size equals $\alpha$ and randomisation is used for discrete data. It is a most powerful test for simple versus simple.

stem: What does it mean for a level-$\alpha$ test to be uniformly most powerful (UMP) for $H_0:\theta\in\Theta_0$ against $H_1:\theta\in\Theta_1$?
correct: Its power at every $\theta\in\Theta_1$ is at least that of every other level-$\alpha$ test.
No other level-$\alpha$ test has higher power at any alternative.

distractors.text: Its power at every $\theta\in\Theta_1$ is at least $1-\alpha$.
distractors.misconception: confuses power with confidence level

distractors.text: Its power at one fixed alternative $\theta_1$ is the largest.
distractors.misconception: most powerful only at a point, not uniformly

distractors.text: Its size is smaller than that of any other level-$\alpha$ test.
distractors.misconception: confuses power with size

distractors.text: Its power function is at least $\alpha$ everywhere on $\Theta_1$, but not necessarily maximal.
distractors.misconception: describes unbiasedness

distractors.text: Its power takes the same value at every point of $\Theta_1$.
distractors.misconception: confuses with a constant power function

explanation: UMP means best simultaneously for all alternatives. A UMP test is a most powerful test for each simple alternative with the same critical region; unbiasedness is a weaker property.

stem: Suppose the family has nondecreasing monotone likelihood ratio in $T(X)$, and consider $H_0:\theta\le\theta_0$ against $H_1:\theta>\theta_0$. What is the UMP test of level $\alpha$ (Karlin-Rubin)?
correct: Reject for $T>c$, randomising at $T=c$ if needed, with size $\alpha$ at $\theta_0$.
A one-sided threshold on $T$ with size $\alpha$ is UMP.

distractors.text: Reject when $T(X)<c$, since a small value indicates a large $\theta$.
distractors.misconception: gets the direction wrong when the ratio increases in $T$

distractors.text: Reject when $|T(X)-E_{\theta_0}T|>c$, which is UMP for one-sided alternatives.
distractors.misconception: uses a two-sided region for a one-sided problem

distractors.text: The test is UMP only for simple $H_0:\theta=\theta_0$ and not for composite $H_0:\theta\le\theta_0$.
distractors.misconception: ignores that the power is monotone, so the size is attained at $\theta_0$

distractors.text: A UMP test exists only for normal families.
distractors.misconception: the MLR property suffices

distractors.text: Reject when $T(X)>c$, with $c$ chosen so that the type II error at $\theta_0$ equals $\alpha$.
distractors.misconception: calibrates the wrong error probability

explanation: MLR makes the power function nondecreasing in $\theta$, so the size over $\theta\le\theta_0$ is controlled at $\theta_0$. The NP test for $\theta_0$ against any $\theta_1>\theta_0$ has the same one-sided region.

stem: For $X\sim N(\theta,1)$, why is there no UMP test of $H_0:\theta=\theta_0$ against $H_1:\theta\ne\theta_0$ at level $\alpha$?
correct: The best tests for each side of $\theta_0$ reject in opposite directions.
The one-sided optimal tests conflict, one rejecting low and one high.

distractors.text: The Neyman-Pearson lemma does not apply to normal families.
distractors.misconception: the lemma applies to every simple pair

distractors.text: The family lacks monotone likelihood ratio in any statistic.
distractors.misconception: it has MLR; the issue is the two-sided alternative

distractors.text: A test of size exactly $\alpha$ cannot be constructed for a continuous variable.
distractors.misconception: size $\alpha$ is easily attained

distractors.text: Every two-sided test has power below $\alpha$ somewhere on the alternative.
distractors.misconception: equal-tailed tests are unbiased with power above $\alpha$

distractors.text: A two-sided UMP test could exist only if the sample space were discrete.
distractors.misconception: discreteness is irrelevant

explanation: Each one-sided UMP test is more powerful than any two-sided test on its own side but has power below $\alpha$ on the other side. Imposing unbiasedness leads to the UMPU two-sided test.

stem: A one-parameter exponential family has density $h(x)\exp\{\eta(\theta)T(x)-A(\theta)\}$. When does it have monotone likelihood ratio in $T$?
correct: When $\eta(\theta)$ is nondecreasing in $\theta$.
Increasing $\eta$ gives MLR in $T$.

distractors.text: When $\eta(\theta)$ is concave in $\theta$.
distractors.misconception: concavity is irrelevant; monotonicity is required

distractors.text: When $T$ is a bounded statistic.
distractors.misconception: boundedness does not matter

distractors.text: For every continuous $\eta(\theta)$ regardless of its shape.
distractors.misconception: a nonmonotone $\eta$ destroys MLR

distractors.text: Only when $\eta(\theta)=\theta$ exactly.
distractors.misconception: any monotone transformation suffices

distractors.text: When $T$ is a complete statistic, since completeness yields a monotone ratio.
distractors.misconception: confuses completeness with MLR

explanation: The ratio $f_{\theta_2}/f_{\theta_1}=\exp\{(\eta(\theta_2)-\eta(\theta_1))T-\dots\}$ is increasing in $T$ iff $\eta(\theta_2)>\eta(\theta_1)$ for $\theta_2>\theta_1$. A decreasing $\eta$ gives MLR in $-T$.

stem: What is an unbiased level-$\alpha$ test of $H_0:\theta\in\Theta_0$ against $H_1:\theta\in\Theta_1$?
correct: A test whose power function is at most $\alpha$ on $\Theta_0$ and at least $\alpha$ on $\Theta_1$ everywhere.
Its power never falls below $\alpha$ anywhere in $H_1$.

distractors.text: A test whose power on $\Theta_1$ is at least $1-\alpha$.
distractors.misconception: confuses unbiasedness with high power

distractors.text: A test that has the same power at every point of the parameter space.
distractors.misconception: confuses with a constant power function

distractors.text: A test with type I error probability exactly zero.
distractors.misconception: confuses with a trivial test

distractors.text: A test that is uniformly most powerful among all level-$\alpha$ tests.
distractors.misconception: confuses unbiasedness with UMP

distractors.text: A test whose rejection region does not depend on the observed data at all.
distractors.misconception: confuses unbiased with trivial tests

explanation: Unbiasedness requires the chance of rejecting a false null to be at least the size. The trivial test $\phi\equiv\alpha$ is unbiased, so a UMP test, which beats it, is automatically unbiased.

stem: In a one-parameter exponential family, which description fits the UMP unbiased test of $H_0:\theta=\theta_0$ against $H_1:\theta\ne\theta_0$?
correct: Reject when $T<c_1$ or $T>c_2$, with size $\alpha$ and zero power slope at $\theta_0$ (unbiasedness).
A two-tailed region on $T$ with unbiased cut-offs.

distractors.text: It rejects only when $T$ is large, as in the one-sided UMP test.
distractors.misconception: uses the one-sided region

distractors.text: It always puts probability $\alpha/2$ in each tail under $\theta_0$.
distractors.misconception: equal tails are correct only for symmetric null distributions

distractors.text: It is the same test for every family, rejecting for $|T|>z_{\alpha/2}$.
distractors.misconception: assumes a normal cut-off for all families

distractors.text: It is not unbiased, which is why it can be uniformly more powerful than any unbiased test.
distractors.misconception: misreads the optimality: the best is over unbiased tests

distractors.text: It is UMP as well, because two-sided UMP tests always exist in exponential families.
distractors.misconception: no UMP test exists for two-sided alternatives

explanation: The power function is minimised at $\theta_0$ for an unbiased test, so its derivative there is zero. This fixes the cut-offs, which are tail-symmetric only for symmetric null distributions of $T$.

stem: Why is a UMP level-$\alpha$ test, when it exists, automatically unbiased?
correct: It beats the trivial test $\phi\equiv\alpha$, so its power is at least $\alpha$ everywhere on $\Theta_1$.
It beats the trivial test $\phi\equiv\alpha$ in power, so it is unbiased.

distractors.text: UMP tests are never unbiased, since they sacrifice power on one side.
distractors.misconception: reverses the relationship

distractors.text: Unbiasedness is part of the definition of a UMP test.
distractors.misconception: unbiasedness is not required in the definition

distractors.text: Only two-sided UMP tests are unbiased, since one-sided ones are biased.
distractors.misconception: one-sided UMP tests are also unbiased

distractors.text: A UMPU test is always UMP, because adding a restriction cannot lower power.
distractors.misconception: reverses the logic: restriction makes UMPU weaker

distractors.text: UMP tests are unbiased only when the null hypothesis is simple.
distractors.misconception: invents an unnecessary condition

explanation: The randomised test $\phi\equiv\alpha$ has level $\alpha$ and power $\alpha$ everywhere, so a UMP test has power $\ge\alpha$ on $\Theta_1$. The converse fails: UMPU tests need not be UMP.

stem: Why condition on a sufficient statistic for the nuisance parameter when testing a hypothesis about the parameter of interest?
correct: Given it, the null law is free of the nuisance parameter, so the size is exact.
It removes the nuisance parameter from the null law.

distractors.text: It raises power at every alternative compared with unconditional tests.
distractors.misconception: conditioning is for exact size, not guaranteed power

distractors.text: It turns the composite alternative into a simple alternative.
distractors.misconception: the alternative stays composite

distractors.text: It discards all information about the parameter of interest.
distractors.misconception: the conditional law keeps that information

distractors.text: It makes the test asymptotic, with size $\alpha$ only in large samples.
distractors.misconception: conditional tests are exact in finite samples

distractors.text: Conditioning guarantees that the test is also UMP unconditionally for every nuisance value.
distractors.misconception: overclaims optimality from conditioning

explanation: Conditioning gives a similar test: size $\alpha$ for every value of the nuisance parameter. For exponential families, conditional tests based on the complementary statistic yield UMPU tests.

stem: In a $2\times2$ table with row and column totals held fixed, what is the null distribution of one cell count when the two classifications are independent?
correct: Hypergeometric, which is the basis of Fisher's exact test for the table.
The count has a hypergeometric law given the margins.

distractors.text: Binomial with success probability $1/2$ and as many trials as the table total.
distractors.misconception: confuses with comparing two Poisson counts

distractors.text: Normal for every table size, because counts are sums.
distractors.misconception: replaces an exact law by an asymptotic one

distractors.text: Poisson with mean equal to the product of the margins over the total.
distractors.misconception: ignores the fixed margins

distractors.text: Uniform over all integers from zero to the table total.
distractors.misconception: ignores the constraint from the margins

distractors.text: Geometric, with success probability equal to the proportion in the first row.
distractors.misconception: confuses with waiting-time laws

explanation: Fixing the margins removes the nuisance parameters (the marginal probabilities), and the cell count becomes hypergeometric under independence. The exact test is conditional.

stem: How is a confidence set obtained by inverting a family of tests?
correct: Gather all $\theta_0$ that the level-$\alpha$ test of $H_0:\theta=\theta_0$ does not reject for the observed $x$.
The $\theta_0$ values not rejected by the test at level $\alpha$.

distractors.text: Collect all $\theta_0$ that the level-$\alpha$ test of $H_0:\theta=\theta_0$ rejects at the observed $x$.
distractors.misconception: takes the rejection set instead of the acceptance set

distractors.text: Collect the values $\theta_0$ at which the p-value equals exactly $\alpha$.
distractors.misconception: takes the boundary instead of the acceptance region

distractors.text: Take all $\theta_0$ for which $\theta_0$ equals the maximum likelihood estimate.
distractors.misconception: uses a point estimate

distractors.text: The set has coverage $\alpha$ because it is built from tests of size $\alpha$.
distractors.misconception: confuses coverage $1-\alpha$ with size

distractors.text: The set of $\theta_0$ where the likelihood is at least half of its maximum value.
distractors.misconception: uses an arbitrary threshold instead of a test

explanation: A test of level $\alpha$ accepts the true $\theta$ with probability at least $1-\alpha$, so the acceptance set has coverage at least $1-\alpha$. The set is random through $x$.

stem: What does inverting a UMP one-sided test of $H_0:\theta\le\theta_0$ give?
correct: A uniformly most accurate lower confidence bound at level $1-\alpha$.
A UMA lower confidence bound, the most accurate at that level.

distractors.text: The shortest possible two-sided interval for $\theta$.
distractors.misconception: confuses accuracy with length of two-sided intervals

distractors.text: The Wald interval, because both rely on the MLE.
distractors.misconception: the Wald interval is an approximate normal-theory interval

distractors.text: A Bayesian credible bound with posterior probability $1-\alpha$.
distractors.misconception: confuses duality with posterior probability

distractors.text: An interval that is always unbiased and two-sided.
distractors.misconception: one-sided bounds are not two-sided intervals

distractors.text: A confidence interval whose length is the smallest possible at every parameter value.
distractors.misconception: confuses accuracy with length

explanation: Optimality transfers by duality: a UMP test gives a confidence bound which, among all bounds of the same level, is least likely to include false values of $\theta$.

stem: How does an interval from inverting the likelihood ratio test differ from the Wald interval?
correct: It can be asymmetric and is reparametrization invariant.
It follows the shape of the likelihood, not a normal approximation.

distractors.text: It is always symmetric about the MLE, like the Wald interval.
distractors.misconception: ignores the asymmetric likelihood shape

distractors.text: It requires the Fisher information to be computed.
distractors.misconception: only needs the likelihood

distractors.text: It is not invariant: reparametrizing $\theta$ changes the set of accepted values.
distractors.misconception: the Wald interval is not invariant, the LR interval is

distractors.text: It is always wider than the Wald interval.
distractors.misconception: no such ordering holds in general

distractors.text: Its coverage is exact in every finite sample, whereas the Wald interval is only approximate.
distractors.misconception: the LR interval is also approximate

explanation: The set $\{\theta:2\{\ell(\hat\theta)-\ell(\theta)\}\le\chi^2_{1,1-\alpha}\}$ follows the likelihood and maps to the set for $g(\theta)$ under reparametrization. The Wald interval depends on the scale used.

stem: What does "95% confidence" for an interval computed from the data actually mean?
correct: 95% of intervals built this way over repeated samples cover $\theta$.
Long-run coverage frequency of the interval-producing method.

distractors.text: The probability that $\theta$ lies in the realised interval is 0.95.
distractors.misconception: treats $\theta$ as random after seeing the data

distractors.text: 95% of the sample observations lie inside the interval.
distractors.misconception: confuses with a prediction or tolerance interval

distractors.text: 95% of future sample means fall in this interval.
distractors.misconception: confuses with a prediction interval

distractors.text: The interval contains $\theta$ with posterior probability 0.95.
distractors.misconception: describes a credible interval

distractors.text: 95% of the possible values of the parameter lie inside the realised interval.
distractors.misconception: treats the interval as a statement about a spread of parameter values

explanation: Confidence refers to the random interval before the data are seen. After observing it, $\theta$ is fixed and either inside or not; the 95% describes the method.

stem: What does it mean for a confidence set $C(X)$ to be unbiased at level $1-\alpha$?
correct: True values are covered more often than false values.
It covers the truth at least as often as any false value.

distractors.text: It has coverage exactly $1-\alpha$ at every $\theta$.
distractors.misconception: confuses unbiasedness with exact coverage

distractors.text: It is centred at an unbiased point estimator of $\theta$.
distractors.misconception: confuses with unbiased estimation

distractors.text: It has the shortest expected length among intervals of that level.
distractors.misconception: confuses with optimality in length

distractors.text: Every confidence interval derived from a test is unbiased.
distractors.misconception: only tests that are unbiased give unbiased sets

distractors.text: It contains false values of $\theta$ with higher probability than the true value.
distractors.misconception: reverses the unbiasedness inequality

explanation: By duality, a set is unbiased iff the corresponding tests are unbiased. UMPU tests give uniformly most accurate unbiased confidence sets.

stem: Under regularity conditions with an interior true parameter, what is the limit law of $-2\log\Lambda_n$ when $H_0$ restricts $r$ of the $d$ free parameters?
correct: A chi-square law whose degrees of freedom equal the difference in the number of free parameters, here $r$.
$\chi^2_r$, with $r$ the dimension of the full model minus that of the null model.

distractors.text: A chi-square law with $d$ degrees of freedom, the dimension of the full parameter space.
distractors.misconception: uses the full dimension instead of the difference

distractors.text: A normal law with mean zero and variance $r$, because the log-likelihood is a sum of terms.
distractors.misconception: applies the central limit theorem to the statistic without squaring

distractors.text: A chi-square law with $n-d$ degrees of freedom, as for a residual sum of squares.
distractors.misconception: imports the regression degrees of freedom

distractors.text: A chi-square law with $r$ degrees of freedom, but only when the data come from a normal model.
distractors.misconception: restricts a general theorem to Gaussian data

distractors.text: A chi-square law whose degrees of freedom grow with the sample size $n$ under the null.
distractors.misconception: confuses the dimension of the model with the sample size

explanation: Wilks theorem gives $-2\log\Lambda_n\to\chi^2_r$ in distribution, with $r$ the number of free parameters in the full model minus the null model, for any regular family and an interior true value.

stem: Which situation can make the chi-square limit of $-2\log\Lambda_n$, with degrees of freedom equal to the difference in dimension, fail?
correct: The true parameter lies on the boundary of the parameter space, for instance a variance component tested against zero.
A boundary null value, where the limit becomes a mixture of chi-square laws.

distractors.text: The null model is a smooth subfamily of the full model and the true parameter is an interior point.
distractors.misconception: treats the regular nested case as a failure

distractors.text: The likelihood is not Gaussian, since Wilks theorem is specific to normal models and nothing else.
distractors.misconception: restricts the theorem to Gaussian likelihoods

distractors.text: The null hypothesis is simple, so the denominator of the ratio has no free parameter to maximise.
distractors.misconception: believes a simple null removes the asymptotics

distractors.text: The null model differs from the full model by several parameters instead of by a single one.
distractors.misconception: believes more than one restriction breaks the theorem

distractors.text: The maximum likelihood estimates have to be found numerically instead of by a closed formula.
distractors.misconception: confuses the form of the estimator with the regularity conditions

explanation: Wilks theorem needs the true value to be interior and the models nested and regular. A true value on the boundary, or a non-nested pair, gives a different limit, typically a mixture such as $\tfrac12\chi^2_0+\tfrac12\chi^2_1$.

stem: How do the Wald and score tests relate to the likelihood ratio test in a regular model with an interior true parameter?
correct: Under $H_0$ the three statistics differ by $o_P(1)$, so each has the same $\chi^2$ limit.
They are asymptotically equivalent alternatives, with a common chi-square limit under the null.

distractors.text: The score test needs the unrestricted fit, while the Wald test is computed from the null fit alone.
distractors.misconception: swaps which fit each statistic uses

distractors.text: The three statistics are exactly equal in every finite sample whenever the model is regular.
distractors.misconception: confuses asymptotic equivalence with finite-sample equality

distractors.text: The Wald test is invariant to reparametrization, unlike the likelihood ratio test.
distractors.misconception: reverses which of the two is invariant

distractors.text: Only the likelihood ratio statistic has a chi-square limit, the other two having model-dependent limits.
distractors.misconception: believes Wald and score limits depend on the model

distractors.text: The three statistics have different degrees of freedom, so they cannot share one critical value.
distractors.misconception: believes equivalence fails for the degrees of freedom

explanation: The Wald statistic uses the unrestricted MLE and the score statistic the null fit only; all three share the $\chi^2_r$ limit and differ by $o_P(1)$. Only the likelihood ratio test is reparametrization invariant.

stem: For a parameter vector $\theta$ of dimension $d$, how is an approximate $1-\alpha$ confidence set obtained by inverting the asymptotic likelihood ratio test?
correct: Keep every $\theta_0$ with $2\{\ell(\hat\theta)-\ell(\theta_0)\}\le\chi^2_{d,1-\alpha}$, the chi-square quantile on $d$ degrees of freedom.
The $\theta_0$ whose log-likelihood is within $\tfrac12\chi^2_{d,1-\alpha}$ of the maximum.

distractors.text: Keep every $\theta_0$ with $2\{\ell(\hat\theta)-\ell(\theta_0)\}\ge\chi^2_{d,1-\alpha}$, the values the test rejects.
distractors.misconception: reverses the inequality and keeps rejected values

distractors.text: Keep every $\theta_0$ with $\ell(\hat\theta)-\ell(\theta_0)\le\chi^2_{d,1-\alpha}$, without the factor two.
distractors.misconception: drops the factor two in the statistic

distractors.text: Keep every $\theta_0$ below the quantile $\chi^2_{1,1-\alpha}$, with one degree of freedom whatever $d$ is.
distractors.misconception: uses one degree of freedom for a vector parameter

distractors.text: The set has coverage exactly $1-\alpha$ at every $n$, since each test of $\theta_0$ has exact size $\alpha$.
distractors.misconception: treats an asymptotic size as an exact size

distractors.text: The set is always $\hat\theta\pm z_{1-\alpha/2}/\sqrt{nI(\hat\theta)}$, the Wald interval, in every model.
distractors.misconception: treats the likelihood set as always equal to the symmetric Wald interval

explanation: The test of $\theta=\theta_0$ rejects when $-2\log\Lambda_n>\chi^2_{d,1-\alpha}$, so the accepted values form the set. Its coverage tends to $1-\alpha$, and it follows the shape of the likelihood.

stem: What is the plug-in principle behind the bootstrap?
correct: Replace $F$ by the empirical cdf $\hat F_n$ and evaluate the target under $\hat F_n$.
Treat the empirical distribution as if it were the population.

distractors.text: Replace $F$ by a fitted normal distribution and compute the quantity analytically.
distractors.misconception: confuses with parametric normal approximation

distractors.text: Replace the sample by its population mean and resample from that.
distractors.misconception: misunderstands what is resampled

distractors.text: Draw new observations from the true $F$ for the standard error.
distractors.misconception: F is unknown

distractors.text: Resample without replacement to obtain a different sample of the same size.
distractors.misconception: without replacement gives the same data back

distractors.text: Replace the statistic by its linear approximation and apply the delta method.
distractors.misconception: confuses the bootstrap with the delta method

explanation: The nonparametric bootstrap approximates the sampling distribution of $\hat\theta(X_1,\dots,X_n)$ under $F$ by that under $\hat F_n$, which is simulated by drawing $n$ points with replacement.

stem: How is a bootstrap standard error of an estimator $\hat\theta$ computed from $B$ resamples?
correct: Standard deviation of the resampled estimates $\hat\theta^{*b}$.
The spread of the resampled estimates.

distractors.text: Divide the standard deviation of the $B$ values $\hat\theta^{*b}$ by $\sqrt B$.
distractors.misconception: confuses with Monte Carlo error of the mean

distractors.text: Take the standard deviation of the original data and divide by $\sqrt n$.
distractors.misconception: gives the standard error of the mean only

distractors.text: Use resamples of size $n/2$ drawn without replacement.
distractors.misconception: wrong resample size and scheme

distractors.text: Take the average of the $B$ values $\hat\theta^{*b}$.
distractors.misconception: the average estimates the expected value, not the spread

distractors.text: Take the standard deviation across the resamples and multiply it by $\sqrt n$.
distractors.misconception: rescales a quantity that is already a standard error

explanation: The bootstrap standard error is $\{\frac1{B-1}\sum_b(\hat\theta^{*b}-\bar\theta^*)^2\}^{1/2}$. $B$ controls only the simulation error; it does not shrink the statistical error.

stem: What is the bootstrap estimate of the bias of $\hat\theta$?
correct: The average of the bootstrap values $\hat\theta^{*b}$ minus the original estimate $\hat\theta$.
Mean of bootstrap values minus the original estimate.

distractors.text: The original estimate $\hat\theta$ minus the average of the bootstrap values.
distractors.misconception: sign reversed

distractors.text: The average of the bootstrap values minus the true value $\theta$.
distractors.misconception: the true value is unknown

distractors.text: The variance of the bootstrap values $\hat\theta^{*b}$.
distractors.misconception: confuses bias with variance

distractors.text: The bias-corrected estimator is $\bar\theta^*$, the average of the bootstrap values.
distractors.misconception: the corrected estimator is $2\hat\theta-\bar\theta^*$

distractors.text: Zero for every statistic, since resampling from the data is unbiased.
distractors.misconception: true for the sample mean only

explanation: The bias $E_F\hat\theta-\theta$ is estimated by $E_{\hat F}\hat\theta^*-\hat\theta$. The corrected estimate is $\hat\theta-(\bar\theta^*-\hat\theta)=2\hat\theta-\bar\theta^*$.

stem: Why does the nonparametric bootstrap fail for the sample maximum of a $U(0,\theta)$ sample?
correct: The bootstrap law has an atom of mass about $0.63$ at the observed maximum.
The bootstrap law puts an atom at the sample maximum.

distractors.text: The sample size is too small, and the bootstrap works once $n$ is large enough.
distractors.misconception: no sample size repairs this

distractors.text: The maximum has infinite variance, so its bootstrap law is undefined.
distractors.misconception: the maximum has finite variance

distractors.text: The number of resamples $B$ must be larger than $n^2$.
distractors.misconception: the failure is not a simulation issue

distractors.text: The maximum is biased downward, and bootstrap cannot handle biased estimators.
distractors.misconception: bias alone does not cause failure

distractors.text: The bootstrap fails for every estimator other than the sample mean.
distractors.misconception: overgeneralises; it works for smooth statistics

explanation: The probability that a resample contains the observed maximum is $1-(1-1/n)^n\to1-e^{-1}$. The bootstrap law of $n(\theta_{\max}-\max^*)$ is not consistent: the statistic is not smooth in $F$.

stem: For the sample mean with finite variance $\sigma^2$, what does bootstrap consistency say?
correct: Given the data, $\sqrt n(\bar X^*-\bar X)$ has the same limit $N(0,\sigma^2)$ as $\sqrt n(\bar X-\mu)$.
The centred bootstrap mean mimics the true law.

distractors.text: It holds only when the population is normal.
distractors.misconception: needs only a finite variance

distractors.text: It requires the variance to be infinite so that the mean is not degenerate.
distractors.misconception: the opposite condition

distractors.text: The bootstrap distribution of $\bar X^*$ is centred at the population mean $\mu$.
distractors.misconception: it is centred at $\bar X$

distractors.text: It requires the number of resamples to equal the sample size $n$.
distractors.misconception: $B$ is only a simulation size

distractors.text: The bootstrap law is wider than the true law by a factor tending to $\sqrt2$.
distractors.misconception: no such inflation occurs

explanation: The bootstrap law of $\bar X^*$ is centred at $\bar X$, so the centred and scaled version mimics $\sqrt n(\bar X-\mu)$. Consistency here follows from the CLT and needs only a finite variance.
